subject: latent growth model: control for time invariant covariate

messages.author: d68921926556beaf
messages.subject: latent growth model: control for time invariant covariate
parts:
Hello,

I'm trying to examine changes in job demand over 3 data waves, and I want to control for organizational group (categorical) for this analysis.
I just wanted to clarify that my syntax is correct to do this.
OG is the categorical exogenous variable. I coded it 0, 1, 2. Lavaan tutorial tells me that I don't need to order the variable if it's exogenous variable.
Thank you so much. I greatly appreciate your support.

model <- '
  # intercept and slope with fixed coefficients
    i =~ 1*JD1 + 1*JD2 + 1*JD3
    s =~ 0*JD1 + 1*JD2 + 2*JD3
   
    i ~ OG # control for time invariant covariate
    s ~ OG

'
fit <- growth(model, data = diss)

messages.author: 82889e926eb5165e
messages.subject: Re: latent growth model: control for time invariant covariate
parts:
There is no need to do anything else if the coavriate is binary (0, 1). Given that is a categorical variable with more than 2 groups, I would recommend one of two options
1. Create 2 dummy code variables based on your 2 groups, like OG_0 (1,0,0), OG_1 (0,1,0). In this case the baseline group would be 2
2. Use the OG variable as a grouping variable, and run the growth model for each category group

messages.author: ad188126f9138663
messages.subject: Re: latent growth model: control for time invariant covariate
parts:
Michelle,
  If you are unfamiliar with the concept of dummy coding, you can find a detailed presentation with examples in the regression/correlation text by Cohen, Cohen, West & Aiken.

  It is not clear why you think that it matters whether the categorical variable is time varying or not.

  Either way, you want to create two new variables such that they flag unique values of OG.  If you want to compare everyone to the OG = 2 group, then compute OG0 such that OG0 = 1 iff OG = 0, and otherwise OG0 = 0.  Likewise, compute OG1 such that OG1 = 1 iff OG = 1, and otherwise OG1 = 0.  You can check your work with contingency tables.  Everyone in the OG = 2 group should have both OG0 and OG1 equal to zero.  Remove OG from your model and replace it with OG0 and OG1 (or their counterparts if you choose a different reference group).  If OG were time varying, you would need to repeat this process for each OG variable.  Because it is time invariant, you should only have one OG variable and only need to do this once.

  The reason that it is okay to treat binary variable as numeric but not categorical variables with more than two values is that the key assumption is that all the intervals that are equal in numeric value are also equal in the differences that they represent.  Because binary variables have only two values, they have only one difference, and it has to be equal to itself.  However, as soon as you introduce three or more values, this no longer holds.  The difference between group 0 and group 1 may not equal the difference between group 1 and group 2.

Keith
------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/

messages.author: ad188126f9138663
messages.subject: Re: latent growth model: control for time invariant covariate
parts:
Michelle,
Two additional comments on your question:

First, bear in mind that the Lavaan model specification syntax is its own syntax distinct from model formulae used elsewhere in R.  That is why, for instance, the asterisk can mean something different in each.

Second, dummy codes have the unusual property of structural zeros because the values are mutually exclusive.  In your case, you have three groups, and four combinations of values on the two dummy codes.  As such, one such combination remains unused.  If you code the dummy variables as flags for a given value, then you have group 1 (1,0), group 2 (0,1), and group 3 (0,0).  However, you have no cases with the combination 1,1.  As a consequence, if you were to compute an interaction term as the product, it would be a constant, always equal to zero.  Alternatively, if you had coded group 3 as 1,1, then the product term would be a group 3 indicator, which is redundant because a case is in group 3 iff it is not in either group 1 or group 2.  Basically, your two dummy variables encode everything that there is to know about your three-valued variable.  There is no further information for a product term to encode.

Keith
------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/

On Saturday, February 15, 2020 at 9:59:30 AM UTC-6, Nickname wrote:
Michelle,
  If you are unfamiliar with the concept of dummy coding, you can find a detailed presentation with examples in the regression/correlation text by Cohen, Cohen, West & Aiken.

  It is not clear why you think that it matters whether the categorical variable is time varying or not.

  Either way, you want to create two new variables such that they flag unique values of OG.  If you want to compare everyone to the OG = 2 group, then compute OG0 such that OG0 = 1 iff OG = 0, and otherwise OG0 = 0.  Likewise, compute OG1 such that OG1 = 1 iff OG = 1, and otherwise OG1 = 0.  You can check your work with contingency tables.  Everyone in the OG = 2 group should have both OG0 and OG1 equal to zero.  Remove OG from your model and replace it with OG0 and OG1 (or their counterparts if you choose a different reference group).  If OG were time varying, you would need to repeat this process for each OG variable.  Because it is time invariant, you should only have one OG variable and only need to do this once.

  The reason that it is okay to treat binary variable as numeric but not categorical variables with more than two values is that the key assumption is that all the intervals that are equal in numeric value are also equal in the differences that they represent.  Because binary variables have only two values, they have only one difference, and it has to be equal to itself.  However, as soon as you introduce three or more values, this no longer holds.  The difference between group 0 and group 1 may not equal the difference between group 1 and group 2.

Michelle,
Two additional comments on your question:

First, bear in mind that the Lavaan model specification syntax is its own syntax distinct from model formulae used elsewhere in R.  That is why, for instance, the asterisk can mean something different in each.

Second, dummy codes have the unusual property of structural zeros because the values are mutually exclusive.  In your case, you have three groups, and four combinations of values on the two dummy codes.  As such, one such combination remains unused.  If you code the dummy variables as flags for a given value, then you have group 1 (1,0), group 2 (0,1), and group 3 (0,0).  However, you have no cases with the combination 1,1.  As a consequence, if you were to compute an interaction term as the product, it would be a constant, always equal to zero.  Alternatively, if you had coded group 3 as 1,1, then the product term would be a group 3 indicator, which is redundant because a case is in group 3 iff it is not in either group 1 or group 2.  Basically, your two dummy variables encode everything that there is to know about your three-valued variable.  There is no further information for a product term to encode.
